source.title: Discover-then-Name: Task-Agnostic Concept Bottlenecks via Automated Concept Discovery
source.authors: Sukrut Rao; S. Mahajan; Moritz Böhle; B. Schiele

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates whether model representations yield human-interpretable concepts using SAE features and human ratings, and compares these with CLIP feature neurons. This is a different measurement and setting from the claim’s neuron-pole audit.
record.gate_note: The paper does not audit Qwen neuron poles or test whether explanations predict activations on held-out inputs. Its user study directly rates the semantic consistency and naming of SAE concepts and CLIP feature neurons, which bears on V4’s tool-related interpretability claim. Classification and intervention results concern the resulting CBMs, not neuron interpretability, so they are not rows. The SUNAttributes Jaccard comparison measures concept-label agreement and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: This is a concept-bottleneck methods paper. It trains SAEs on pooled CLIP output embeddings, names the SAE latents, and reports how well its own method performs. It does not audit a model's own neurons, estimate a share of interpretable neurons, or vary architecture or explanation tools for neurons. Its only raw-neuron data is a small side baseline: 9 dimensions of CLIP ResNet-50's 1024-d pooled output embedding, named with CLIP-Dissect and rated by 22 internal respondents. That data is reported only as a figure and is framed as method-versus-baseline. Those dimensions come from a projected embedding, not hidden-layer neurons, so they cannot show V4's tool- or architecture-dependent share. The paper assumes the opposite premise to the claim (raw features are 'typically uninterpretable', citing Elhage et al.) without testing it.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAEs on CLIP features discover semantically consistent concepts that can be named automatically, and that these yield performant, task-agnostic CBMs. They add that SAE concepts were rated significantly more consistent than raw CLIP features, and that some low-alignment concepts are not human-interpretable or are misnamed because of vocabulary limits.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains sparse autoencoders on CLIP image features, names their latent dictionary features with CLIP text embeddings, and rates concepts with human judgments; it does not audit positive and negative sides of individual neurons as in the claim’s Qwen audit.
record.method_sensitivity: Human-rated semantic consistency varies with feature-to-name alignment; the paper states it decreases as alignment decreases. Naming quality is also discussed as dependent on vocabulary granularity.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 22-respondent internal user study, SAE latents on CLIP ResNet-50 pooled output features were rated more semantically consistent and better named than raw output-embedding dimensions named with CLIP-Dissect (15 vs 9 units, figure-only). Consistency fell with lower name alignment for both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents on a vision-language embedding are rated more human-interpretable than the raw embedding dimensions under the same top-image inspection.

fits_no_version.finding: Mapping SAE latents to SUNAttributes labels gives a Jaccard index of 18.3, versus 22.0 for CLIP retrieval from ground-truth attributes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-discovered visual concepts agree moderately with human attribute labels, below a retrieval baseline.

record.problems: The human evaluation samples only 15 SAE nodes and 9 CLIP feature neurons; 22 survey responses are reported, but numerical ratings and uncertainty estimates are not given in the text. The study evaluates CLIP ResNet-50 features for this user study, not neuron poles across a broad set of language models.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for CBM classification accuracies or Waterbirds interventions: those report downstream classifier performance, not neuron or feature interpretability. Additional qualitative examples and clusters are not independent quantitative measurements of interpretability.

untested.parts: All of it: no Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit.
All of it: no language models are studied.
All of it: no InceptionV1 cat/car neuron and no recursive-generalization analysis.
All of it: no hidden-layer neuron share, and no comparison across explanation tools or architectures for neurons.
All of it: no attribution graphs from the model's own neurons.
All of it: no test of whether explanations predict firing on held-out inputs.
All of it: no simulation-based scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the SAE-vs-raw-feature user study to V4. That link is wrong. SAE latents are a trained replacement basis, not the model's neurons. The raw comparator is the 1024-d pooled output embedding (a projection, not neurons behind a nonlinearity) with only 9 units and figure-only ratings. The study's framing assumes the polysemantic premise the essay disputes, but it supplies no neuron-share test of it. The classification and intervention results are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and its reported proportions of one-job, two-related-job, and not-understood neuron poles.
Similar proportions across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and model scales up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and the proposed shared-pose interpretation or recursive generalization.

The paper compares SAE features with CLIP feature neurons on CLIP ResNet-50, but does not test architecture as a cause, compare modern architectures, or estimate the overall interpretable-neuron share or the InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a replacement model or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations derived from activating examples predict activation on new inputs; the study rates top-activating examples but does not test firing predictions.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
